update description: Specify needs: stakeholder needs identification, option analysis, and business case preparation are increasingly supported by automated and AI-powered processes. impact reasoning: For the Junior Data Analyst, this update shifts part of the role from primarily manual support in gathering, organizing, and consolidating information toward supporting AI-enabled needs analysis workflows. The role will increasingly contribute by preparing structured inputs for automated tools, validating AI-generated summaries or recommendations, checking quality and relevance of stakeholder-derived information, and escalating issues where contextual or ethical judgement is required. Operationally, routine compilation and documentation tasks become more automated. Responsibility correspondingly expands in the direction of critical review of AI-assisted outputs, stronger data and metadata standardization, traceability of inputs used in needs analysis, and clearer support to senior staff in interpreting findings for planning and prioritization. The role remains junior, but the expected contribution becomes more analytical and quality-assurance-oriented, with greater emphasis on human oversight of automated processes than on repetitive manual preparation alone.

update description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. In the modern process, AI and automated tools are used to continuously scan for new information requests from users, detect relevant environmental changes, and aggregate respondent feedback and evaluation action plans. These technologies also benchmark needs by automatically referencing practices among other (national and international) statistical organizations. Automation supports the collation, analysis, and structuring of these triggers for new or changed statistics, while staff focus their expertise on interpreting context, confirming significance, and ensuring response to complex or emergent requirements.
interdependencies: Subsequent downstream design, data sourcing, and analysis activities will increasingly rely on the analyst's early validation of AI-generated needs signals, affecting later work in research, data preparation, methodological selection, and reporting.

impact reasoning: The current work-description already positions the Junior Data Analyst as supporting studies, conducting data preparation, organizing information, attending meetings, and participating in project teams. update description: This sub-process systematically checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. Existing data holdings must be exhaustively investigated and prioritized first, followed by a search for relevant administrative and alternative data sources; the option to conduct new surveys is only considered if these avenues prove insufficient to meet data needs. The subject matter sponsor holds sole accountability for certifying that all relevant avenues for data have been thoroughly explored and that the suitability, timeliness, and quality of any proposed source have been rigorously assessed. To expedite and strengthen the acquisition of administrative and alternative data, a center of expertise works collaboratively with subject matter specialists to support negotiations, acquisition logistics, and the establishment of legal or operational agreements where needed. When multiple avenues have been assessed and documented, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps is prepared. This sub-process also encompasses the assessment and possible updates to the legal framework for data collection, ensuring fit-for-purpose, respondent-efficient, and timely data acquisition and usage.
interdependencies: Upstream dependence on clearly defined user requirements that determine what constitutes suitable, timely, quality-assured source data
Downstream impact on source integration, data validation, processing, and analysis activities because stronger source suitability assessment changes what data are acquired and how they are prepared
Operational dependency on collaboration with subject matter specialists and a center of expertise for administrative/alternative data acquisition, agreements, and legal-operational conditions
impact reasoning: The work-description will shift from a primarily analysis-support role using established data management methods toward a more explicit front-end role in systematically assessing whether existing internal holdings, administrative data, and alternative data sources are fit for purpose before new collection is considered. For a Junior Data Analyst, this means greater involvement in source discovery, structured comparison of candidate sources, validation of AI/automation-enabled checks for source quality, timeliness, coverage, continuity, and restrictions on use, and more rigorous documentation of evidence supporting source suitability. The role will remain junior and supportive rather than accountable for final certification, but expectations will expand to include technical due diligence on data availability and suitability, stronger awareness of legal/privacy/usage constraints, and closer collaboration with specialized acquisition or subject matter functions. The updated work-description would therefore differ by emphasizing digital-first and source-first acquisition logic, documented assessment of existing and external sources, support to administrative/alternative data onboarding, and stronger quality and governance considerations at the point of source selection.

update description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments, and operational processes—with a strong emphasis on automation, AI-powered tools, and digital interoperability. Automated and AI-driven processes play a central role in drafting specifications, aligning with corporate and international standards, generating and enriching metadata, simulating system interactions, and iterating design improvements. All statistical products and their supporting metadata are produced in standardized, richly described, and machine-actionable forms, ensuring they are interoperable and reusable across downstream tools, APIs, and organizational systems. Staff are freed from repetitive and routine design work and instead focus on innovation, calibration, and optimizing for evolving user and stakeholder requirements. Design activities thus promote efficiency, quality, and discoverability, embedding best practices for automation, standardization, and open data access. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes, which can occur in parallel and may be iterative, with iteration between Design and Build supported through automated versioning and process enhancements.

Metadata and standards alignment requirements that affect downstream collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, and evaluation activities

impact reasoning: The current Junior Data Analyst role already supports analytical studies, data preparation, validation, modeling, visualization, and participation in analytics projects using AI and software tools. Under the updated Design phase, the role changes from primarily applying established methods to also validating, quality-assuring, contextualizing, and helping operationalize AI- and automation-generated design components. The role will increasingly interact with standardized, machine-actionable metadata and interoperable design artifacts rather than only manually prepared analytical inputs. Routine design-related work such as drafting specifications, basic metadata preparation, and standards alignment will be partially automated, shifting the analyst's contribution toward reviewing automated outputs, checking fitness for purpose, identifying risks such as bias or standards non-compliance, and calibrating outputs against user, stakeholder, and program needs. This increases the importance of metadata literacy, interoperability concepts, automation oversight, AI quality assurance, and version-aware collaboration with technical and business teams. The role remains junior, but expectations expand from executing data analysis tasks to supporting responsible and reusable design processes across the statistical production lifecycle.

update description: This sub-process defines the variables to be collected via the collection instrument and any that will be derived for analysis or dissemination, with a strong emphasis on standards compliance, automation, and machine-actionability. All variable definitions and supporting metadata must comply with national and international standards (e.g., SDMX), structured in machine-actionable formats and managed through prescribed data management tools (such as Aria or Colectica) to ensure robust lifecycle control and digital traceability. AI/LLM-enabled tools are used to generate, refine, and validate variable names, descriptions, and attributes, maximizing clarity, standardization, and discoverability. Staff involved in this sub-process are proficient in digital metadata standards and tooling, ensuring all variable-related products are interoperable, automation-ready, and reusable by both human and machine users. This ensures that the resulting statistical outputs are consistently described, easily found, and seamlessly integrated across digital platforms and systems.

The work-description would therefore differ by requiring more explicit responsibility for interoperable metadata production, variable naming and attribute standardization, traceable documentation, and validation of definitions against national/international standards. update description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, with a strategic emphasis on automation, AI/ML, and passive acquisition. Where possible, the design must prioritize passive, administrative, and already-available sources of data; surveys or direct solicitation are employed only when all other avenues are exhausted or cannot provide suitable data. All aspects of collection design—including the configuration of instruments, sequencing, respondent communications, and integration agreements—should embed automation, machine-to-machine interfaces, digital event/trigger-based collection, and minimal manual intervention. Where a survey instrument is essential, automated and AI-driven methods must be used for design, rendering, and fielding, ensuring quick turnaround, reduced burden, and full standards compliance. The sub-process also entails the necessary design of respondent management, monitoring, and adaptive feedback loops to maximize efficiency and data quality, while reserving human staff for exception handling and final validation.
interdependencies: 4.1 Collect frame and sample data
4.2 Set up collection
4.3 Run collection
5.1 Integrate data
5.2 Classify and code
5.3 Review and validate
impact reasoning: The current Junior Data Analyst role already supports data acquisition, validation, analysis, and participation in research and analytics projects, but its emphasis is broader and more downstream from collection design. Under this update, the role would shift earlier in the statistical production cycle to support digital-first collection design through technical vetting of passive and administrative data sources, support for API- and machine-to-machine-enabled collection methods, automated quality checks, and monitoring of collection metadata and adaptive feedback signals. The role would increasingly support the design and testing of AI-assisted collection instruments and automated collection workflows rather than mainly analyzing data after receipt. Operationally, the role would perform more structured assessment of source suitability, data exchange mechanisms, standards compliance, respondent burden reduction, and exception-based monitoring. Responsibilities would evolve toward supporting automated collection ecosystems, validating collection logic and interfaces, and providing evidence for when direct collection remains necessary. This also implies stronger requirements in data integration design awareness, metadata handling, collection systems literacy, and understanding of governance, agreements, and privacy constraints for passive and administrative acquisition.

interdependencies: 4.1 Create frame and select sample
End-to-end digital pipeline integration across pre-collection and post-collection processes

impact reasoning: This update shifts the Junior Data Analyst role from primarily applying established data preparation and analysis methods on internally managed datasets toward supporting digitally integrated, quality-by-design sampling preparation processes. The role is affected because frame and sample design now depends on AI-enabled source quality controls, partner-prepared inputs, and seamless integration with automated business pipelines. While the employee remains junior and supportive in scope, they will increasingly be expected to validate frame-related data from administrative, alternative, and partner-held sources; assess whether automated cleaning and quality controls are suitable for downstream use; and contribute evidence and analysis to teams designing more flexible and adaptive sampling approaches. The role therefore evolves from supporting data analysis after data acquisition toward earlier involvement in pre-collection design activities, especially in data quality assessment, metadata interpretation, integration readiness, and monitoring of automated frame-design inputs. This also introduces stronger expectations around documenting data provenance, understanding how frame quality affects later analytic validity, and collaborating with partners and internal teams on digitally standardized frame inputs.

update description: This sub-process designs the statistical methodology to be applied during the Process and Analyse phases, with a core emphasis on standards-based automation, AI enablement, and digital interoperability. Specifications for routines and rules covering coding, editing, imputation, validation, and data integration/estimation are required to be implemented, where practical, using automated frameworks and AI/ML-driven tools—leveraging SDMX models, .STAT processing, and corporate-standard solutions (e.g., Aria/Colectica). Human analysts and methodologists are focused on reviewing and updating analytic methods for non-standard or novel use-cases, with all standardizable and repeatable components digital, automated, and reproducible by default. Statistical disclosure control and quality assurance methods designed here also leverage automation and AI for rapid, secure, and scalable deployment. All methodologies are documented to be compatible with downstream digital workflows and to support auditing, versioning, and continuous improvement.
interdependencies: Process-phase activities that operationalize automated coding, editing, imputation, validation, and integration routines
Analyse-phase activities that depend on reproducible, versioned, and auditable analytical workflows
Corporate data governance, metadata, and interoperability standards used in downstream digital workflows
Quality assurance and statistical disclosure control processes that become increasingly automated and traceable
impact reasoning: The current Junior Data Analyst role already supports data wrangling, validation, modeling, visualization, software development, and AI-assisted problem solving, but the updated sub-process shifts the role from primarily applying established methods to helping implement and sustain standards-based, automated, and reproducible processing and analysis designs. Work will increasingly require configuring and testing automated analytical routines; working within corporate-standard platforms and metadata structures; documenting methods for auditability, versioning, and reuse; and supporting AI-enabled quality assurance, validation, and disclosure control workflows. The role will remain junior in scope, but expectations will move toward stronger operational discipline in reproducible pipeline execution, standards compliance, and method traceability, while human judgment is concentrated on exceptions, anomalies, and non-standard analytical situations. Compared with the current state, the updated work-description would place less emphasis on one-off manual preparation and more emphasis on maintainable automated workflows, metadata-driven processing, quality-controlled AI/ML use, and digital interoperability across downstream processes.

update description: This sub-process determines the workflow from data collection to dissemination, ensuring all production processes are seamlessly integrated, modular, and event-driven, with automation and AI/ML supporting orchestration, monitoring, and transitions. Workflows are designed to minimize manual intervention and maximize real-time coordination, leveraging digital platforms and automation for every routine or standardized task. The emphasis is on building touchless, continuous data pipelines that allow for automated validation, routing, escalation, and exception reporting. Existing automated solutions and system components are reused wherever possible; if new components are needed, they are built automation- and integration-ready from inception. Staff responsibilities focus on system oversight, addressing exceptions and inefficiencies, and iteratively improving and upgrading automated workflows for future resilience and scalability.

Impacts downstream analysis, reporting, and dissemination by increasing reliance on real-time, event-driven workflow outputs, automated quality checks, and exception-handling processes.

update description: This phase describes the processing of input data and their preparation for analysis, using modular, version-controlled, automation- and AI/ML-enabled digital workflows. Every sub-process—integrate, classify, check, clean, and transform input data—is configured for event-driven orchestration, reproducibility, and end-to-end automation wherever feasible, ensuring high speed, quality, and consistency. Routine manipulation, error-checking, cleaning, imputation, and integration are handled by AI-enabled modules, with 50% or more of manual interventions eliminated. All processing operations produce full audit trails and documentation for traceability, enabling rapid adjustment and continuous process improvement. Analysts and staff focus on process oversight, exception handling, and innovation, while ensuring all processed outputs are standardized, metadata-rich, and downstream-ready for analysis and dissemination. The Process phase is broken down into eight sub-processes, which may run sequentially, in parallel, or iteratively, as determined by automated orchestration and analytic requirements.

Under the updated Process phase, the Junior Data Analyst's work shifts materially from manually performing routine processing steps toward configuring, monitoring, validating, and improving modular automated pipelines. update description: Where data are considered incorrect, missing, unreliable, outdated, or duplicated, edits and imputations are made through automated, modular, and AI/LLM-powered digital pipelines. update description: This sub-process derives data for variables and units needed to deliver required outputs using modular, automation- and AI-powered methods. Digital pipelines apply arithmetic and formula-based logic, iterating as needed and recording all derivations and transformations with a traceable audit trail. Manual intervention is reserved for rare, non-standard or complex derivations beyond automation, with staff focusing on validation and insight for exceptions. This structure maximizes efficiency, reproducibility, and transparency in all variable/unit derivation steps.

impact reasoning: The work-description shifts the Junior Data Analyst role away from primarily hands-on, manual derivation of new variables and units toward operating within modular automated derivation pipelines and AI-assisted transformation environments. This changes the operational emphasis from direct derivation execution to pipeline-aware quality assurance, exception handling, reproducibility control, and transparent documentation. The role also evolves to require stronger understanding of derivation governance, metadata, lineage, and explainability, while retaining the need for judgment in assessing non-routine data issues and reliability of transformed outputs.

update description: This sub-process brings together and finalizes the results of all previous sub-processes in the phase, producing data files (micro- or macro-level) in fully standardized, open, and machine-actionable formats by default. All datasets and supporting documentation are versioned, digitally logged, and immediately available for reproducible handoff to subsequent analysis or dissemination phases. Technical staff ensure compliance with standards and continuous skills development, and all processes are supported by automated documentation and audit trails, supporting immediate traceability, interoperability, and readiness for deployment across business domains.
interdependencies: Dependent on upstream data preparation, validation, editing, and transformation activities because finalization now requires standardized outputs, version control, and machine-actionable documentation from earlier processing steps.

Creates downstream impacts for Analyse and Disseminate phases because finalized files must now be reproducible, traceable, interoperable, and immediately usable by analysts and dissemination systems without manual rework.

Closely linked to automation, metadata, quality assurance, and governance practices because automated documentation and audit trails become part of routine file finalization rather than optional supporting work.
impact reasoning: The current work-description already includes data wrangling, validation, analysis, software use, research support, and some participation in AI and data governance activities. However, the role is presently oriented more toward supporting analysis and preparing data for studies than toward formally finalizing standardized production-grade data assets for reproducible organizational handoff. Under update 5.8, the Junior Data Analyst's work would expand from preparing and analyzing data to also ensuring that finalized datasets and related documentation conform to open and machine-actionable standards, are versioned and digitally logged, and are traceable through automated audit mechanisms. This shifts the role toward stronger operational quality assurance, metadata management, standardized technical handoff, and troubleshooting of automated outputs. The updated work-description would therefore differ by making formal data finalization, reproducibility, standards compliance, documentation automation, and audit-readiness explicit expectations rather than implicit or occasional supporting tasks. The role would also require stronger awareness of enterprise data interoperability and deployment readiness across business domains, not just project-level analytical usefulness.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Bullet 1: Supports the conduct of studies and/or projects using quantitative statistical data analysis methods, such as: data wrangling, validation, mining, and visualization (in R/RStudio, Python, SQL, Java, JavaScript or another software), as well as software development, application of machine/deep learning and artificial intelligence techniques for problem solving.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This activity would expand from using analytical methods to also packaging and finalizing outputs in standardized, open, machine-actionable formats suitable for reproducible downstream use. gaps.name: Standards-based data finalization
gaps.description: Ability to prepare and finalize datasets in standardized, open, interoperable, and machine-actionable formats for organizational reuse and downstream automation.

gaps.justification: The update requires immediate reproducible handoff and machine consumption, which exceeds current expectations centered on analysis support.
gaps.name: Open data and interoperability standards
gaps.description: Knowledge of file, schema, metadata, and exchange standards that support reproducibility, interoperability, and machine readability across systems and business domains.

gaps.justification: The updated process requires validation of technical handoff quality, not just analytical processing.
gaps.name: Technical handoff validation
gaps.description: Ability to test finalized files, schemas, metadata, and dependencies to ensure they can be reliably transferred into analysis and dissemination workflows without manual correction.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Bullet 2: Analyses statistical data using established data management methods. Drafts summary analysis of qualitative and/or quantitative data and presents findings and recommendations to colleagues and/or team members.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Analysis work would now be supported by a stronger requirement to verify that the underlying finalized files are versioned, logged, reproducible, and auditable. gaps.justification: The current activity covers data management methods, but the update adds reproducibility and auditability as expected qualities of the analytical inputs.
gaps.name: Reproducible data workflow principles
gaps.description: Knowledge of versioning, provenance, lineage, dependency tracking, and reproducible workflow practices that ensure analysis can be repeated from finalized source files.

gaps.justification: Presenting findings will increasingly require explaining file quality, traceability, and readiness issues to team members.
gaps.name: Data quality communication in production contexts
gaps.description: Ability to communicate issues related to standardization, auditability, lineage, and technical readiness of finalized datasets to technical and non-technical colleagues.

affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This is directly affected because 'work files' would need to evolve into managed, versioned, digitally logged data and documentation assets. gaps.justification: The current wording implies basic file organization, whereas the update requires formal versioned and logged file management.
gaps.name: Version control and file lifecycle management
gaps.description: Ability to manage datasets and supporting documentation using formal versioning, naming conventions, release tracking, and controlled updates.

gaps.justification: The updated description explicitly requires supporting documentation to be finalized and immediately available.
gaps.name: Metadata and documentation authoring
gaps.description: Ability to create and maintain structured metadata, data dictionaries, processing notes, and release documentation sufficient for reproducible handoff.

gaps.justification: The shift from maintaining work files to traceable digital assets requires understanding provenance and logging concepts.
gaps.name: Data provenance and digital logging
gaps.description: Knowledge of how file changes, approvals, timestamps, and processing history are recorded to support traceability and audit requirements.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Bullet 4: Attends Departmental meetings, and interdepartmental and stakeholder meetings (as required), to gather data/information and to optimize the business value of data.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Meetings would increasingly involve clarifying standards, handoff expectations, data structure requirements, interoperability issues, and governance/compliance expectations for finalized outputs. Optimizing business value of data would include ensuring finalized data files are reusable across business domains.

gaps.justification: The update emphasizes interoperability and deployment readiness across business domains, which requires broader standards and governance discussions with stakeholders.
gaps.name: Enterprise data governance and interoperability
gaps.description: Knowledge of organizational data governance expectations, cross-domain reuse requirements, and interoperability considerations for finalized statistical outputs.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Bullet 5: Participates in project teams and working groups to support data management, research and analysis, and other unit activities.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Project participation would now include support to automated documentation, quality gates, file finalization controls, audit readiness, and standards compliance reviews. gaps.justification: The update adds explicit expectations for compliance, automated audit trails, and standardized finalization within team-based workflows.
gaps.name: Collaborative quality assurance in data production
gaps.description: Ability to work within team-based controls for validating outputs, checking standards compliance, and supporting release readiness of finalized datasets.

affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Judgement would need to extend beyond relevance and reliability of sources to include appropriateness of final output formats, metadata sufficiency, traceability requirements, and whether automated documentation and audit records adequately support release and handoff.

gaps.justification: Current judgement criteria focus on source assessment and method selection, not release-readiness and standard-conformance decisions.
gaps.name: Data release readiness criteria
gaps.description: Knowledge of how to assess whether finalized files, metadata, and process records meet organizational requirements for quality, traceability, and downstream use.

affected work-description elements.element: Technical Activities - Bullet 2: The data preparation and analysis supports the work of studies and projects and the development of reports and recommendations presented to management by senior data analysts. affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: The impact of this work would broaden because finalized files now directly affect not only senior analysts' analysis quality but also reproducibility, audit outcomes, and usability by dissemination and other business systems. gaps.justification: The updated process increases consequences of data preparation errors, requiring stronger production-quality discipline.
gaps.name: Production-grade quality control
gaps.description: Ability to apply systematic checks to finalized outputs so they are accurate, complete, standardized, and suitable for operational reuse.

affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Aggregation would now need to culminate in finalized files that are standardized, documented, and traceable, not just valid and reliable for analysis. gaps.justification: The current activity stops at valid and reliable analytical data, while the update requires formally finalized, shareable, auditable outputs.

gaps.justification: Completing the data lifecycle under the updated process requires awareness of engineering-style controls in addition to analysis methods.
gaps.name: End-to-end data lifecycle management
